title: Paulinus of Nola (22 June)
hook: a wealthy poet and senator who gave it up to live simply as a bishop

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aloysius Gonzaga, the heir who nursed the sick of Rome. Your line was young and brave.

A letter arrives from an old teacher. It's elegant, a little hurt, and written in verse. Why have you gone quiet? it asks. Why have you left the life we shared, the estates, the books, the clever friends? The student writes back, also in verse. He hasn't stopped writing poetry. He has changed what it's for. Today, a rich man who gave his fortune away and kept his pen. Paulinus of Nola.
screen: `A LETTER IN VERSE.` → `WHY HAVE YOU GONE QUIET?` → `THE ANSWER, ALSO IN VERSE.`

segments.voice: Paulinus belonged to the comfortable old Roman world. He came from a wealthy family in Gaul, studied with the poet Ausonius, held high office, and owned estates. He married a Spanish woman named Therasia. Then their lives turned. Paulinus was baptized, they lost a baby son, and together they decided to give their wealth away. Not in one dramatic gesture, but by selling and giving, steadily, to the poor and to the Church. Jesus had said it to a rich young man. In the Douay-Rheims: "If thou wilt be perfect, go sell what thou hast, and give to the poor." In the Gospel that man goes away sad. Paulinus and Therasia did it. Their circle was shocked. Ausonius, his old teacher, wrote asking him to come back. Paulinus answered, in poems, that his heart now belonged to Christ, and that the old gods of poetry no longer had a claim on him. He wasn't giving up beauty. He was turning it toward God. The couple settled at Nola, in southern Italy, beside the tomb of a martyr, Saint Felix, whom Paulinus loved. They lived simply and cared for pilgrims and the poor. Later the people of Nola chose Paulinus as their bishop. He wrote to other Christian writers of his time, including Augustine and Jerome. And each year, for the feast of Felix, he wrote a new poem. So the rich official became a poet bishop: not a man who gave up everything he was, but one who handed it over, his money, his marriage and his craft, and let each one be used for something else.
screen: `A RICH ROMAN AND A POET.` · `WITH THERASIA, HE GIVES IT AWAY.` · `POEMS TURNED TOWARD GOD.` · `A BISHOP WHO KEPT WRITING.` · then, large: `GO SELL WHAT THOU HAST, AND GIVE TO THE POOR.`

segments.voice: Let one thing you're grateful for, or one thing you need, come to mind, and find three plain lines for it. Say them silently, then change one word to make them truer. If you pray, let the lines be your prayer today, addressed however you pray; if you don't, keep them as a few honest lines.
Paulinus, the rich Roman official and poet of Nola. With his wife Therasia, he gave his wealth away and became its bishop.
Your line: the poet bishop. A gift can change what it's for without being lost. Day one thousand two, done.

howItsDone: The Church keeps an optional memorial of Saint Paulinus of Nola on 22 June; in Nola his memory is tied to a summer festival, and his poems and letters are read by those who study early Christian writing.

chat.says: A poet who became a bishop? Did he have to give up writing poems?
options: No. He gave his wealth away but kept writing, and turned his poems toward God.
Yes. He burned his poems and never wrote another line once he was baptized.
No, but from then on he wrote poems only for the emperor, as part of his office.
